Cory Whitney

October 06, 2026

1 Introduction

Decisions made under uncertainty occur in circumstances where a decision-maker is in the position of choosing between potentially competing options. Such decisions often have to be made with no formal scientific support and might not need much formal support (Keeney 2004).However, when dealing with complex systems that have long-term impacts such as decisions related to policy development, nutrition, agricultural practices, amongst others, strong formal support based on expert knowledge and scientific evidence becomes important. Uncertainty—arising from incomplete information, variability, and ambiguity—affects how individuals, organizations, and systems make and justify choices. Over time, decision analysis has evolved from deterministic optimization frameworks to probabilistic, participatory, and adaptive approaches that integrate behavioural, computational, and systems perspectives.

Decision-supporting research can offer formal support by prescribing a recommended course of action. In general, this is done with the assumption that decision-makers seek maximum expected utility. This means we must assume that the decision maker will want the option with the greatest positive outcome according to their stated outcomes of interest. The decision-making processes can be categorized into two levels of decision making: 1) a decision aimed at influencing an outcome where the expected choice is the one which maximizes the desired outcome, based on information currently available to the decision maker and 2) a decision on how to allocate resources to reduce the uncertainty in the previous decision problem, i.e., to increase the current information to improve the likelihood of choosing the option with the most beneficial outcome.

Such decisions are often made in policy settings like in healthcare, where a choice to fund the health of one part of society often comes at the cost of another, assuming limited budget allocation (Claxton et al. 2015). This choice involves costs, benefits and risks in the form of possible damage and trade-offs in comparison to a baseline and or other decision options.

Our own work has covered such situations regarding the nutritional costs of agricultural expansion in Uganda (Whitney et al. 2018), the choice between different siltation management options in Burkina Faso (Lanzanova et al. 2019), the management of competing water resources in Kenya (Luedeling et al. 2015), and deciding between agroforestry interventions in Vietnam (Do et al. 2020). In these cases, we apply, adopt and update the classical processes of Decision Analysis (Keeney 1982; Jeffrey 1990; Howard and Abbas 2015). To achieve this, we co-generate impact pathways of decisions to provide the structure for a mathematical formula that is then used to estimate the expected utility. We perform a quantitative analysis (Luedeling et al. 2022) of welfare-based decision-making processes using Monte Carlo simulations. In our work, we interpret the welfare-based decision problem as a von Neumann-Morgenstern utility function and apply the ‘Value of Information Analysis’ to assign a value to a certain reduction in uncertainty or, equivalently, increase in information.

There are a number of ways that decisions made under uncertainty can be supported. Through this review we seek to generate a complete overview of all the applications of similar processes that aim to support decision-making under uncertainty.

We offer an overview of methods that are applied to support decisions under uncertainty. We focus on summarizing the state-of-the-art methods in decisions. We identify, define, and evaluate research by extracting the decision-supporting methods, describing them and their approach to supporting decisions. We present a protocol-driven comprehensive review and synthesis of the various methods applied for decision support. We offer an overview of where these methods have been applied. We also offer an interpretation about where these applications can be expanded.

2 Review and Synthesis

3 Protocol-driven approach to reviewing decision support methods

3.1 Literature collection

We gathered data from the Web of Science Core Collection curated database of published, peer-reviewed and larger and more diverse published articles, preprints, theses, books, and other relevant scientific content in Google Scholar and the Centre for Agriculture and Biosciences International (CABI) Digital Library. The final search query consisted of the following keywords.

Web of Science yielded 14 results

Decision + Intervention OR policy + Uncertainty + Expert OR stakeholder + Model OR monte carlo OR simulation OR computer assisted + value of information OR information accuracy

CABI yielded 13 results

Decision + Intervention OR policy + Uncertainty + Expert OR stakeholder + Model OR “monte carlo” OR simulation OR “computer assisted” + “value of information” OR “information accuracy”

Google Scholar yielded 17500+1 results

“decision”+(“intervention”OR”policy”)+“uncertainty”+(“expert”OR”stakeholder”)+(“model”OR”monte carlo”OR”simulation”OR”Bayesian”OR”computer assisted”)+ (“value of information”OR”information accuracy”)2

We collected records in April to July 2023. Associated papers and articles from the search records were also gathered as secondary data collection. Some had shared arXiv or doi links, other parts of shared contributions and assorted affiliations that led to new papers. We screened the collected records to confirm their eligibility for the study.

3.1.1 Inclusion criteria:

  1. Record should be in the English language,
  2. Scientific articles, reports and others are included,
  3. Must involve some form of decision-making or decision-supporting aspect,

3.1.2 Reasons for exclusion

  • Annual reports, syllabus, catalogs of studies, unrelated legal documents, published bibliography collections, duplicates, course notes, preprints (where we already have the published journal article)
  • All non-scientific reports and case studies
(#fig:02_prisma) Overview of the methods review process following the the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA)

We followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) @ref(fig:02_prisma) SystematicReviewOverviewFigure

We preserved our search string on searchRxiv (Whitney 2023)

After importing papers to Zotero we:

  • Ran a native PDF search in Zotero to find missing PDFs.
  • Did a manual PDF search for ~1000 3
  • Remove spurious work that turned up in the results: Annual reports (50+), syllabus / catalogs of studies (100+), unrelated legal documents (30+), published bibliography collections, duplicates (50+), course notes (20), preprints (where we already have the published journal article 50)
  • Add papers to our collection that appear in the bibliography and syllabus that were not already in the search (400+).
  • Formatted meta-data for all references with Linter https://github.com/northword/zotero-format-metadata
  • All manual classification were used to inform automation functions

In looking for the PDFs and following up with some of the thesis, notes, syllabi etc. in the list we added additional associated papers and articles. Some had shared arXiv or doi links, other parts of shared contributions and assorted affiliations that lead to new papers. Sometimes the class notes and syllabus that were in the scholar search return were there because they listed papers that were relevant to our search terms. These were sometimes already in our main collection and sometimes not. When they were not in our collection, we added them.

The Zotero export holds 12,625 records. After duplicate removal and screening, 11,151 records are included (details in the next section).

3.2 Data Import and Preprocessing

3.2.1 Bibliographic Data

All numbers in this section are counted by scripts, not typed. The scripts run in this order (see README.md):

  1. R/prisma_pipeline.R reads the Zotero exports (bib/bib_raw/*.bib), removes duplicates and applies the manual and automatic screening.
  2. R/enrich_records.R fills missing abstracts and DOIs (OpenAlex, Crossref) and checks every DOI against Crossref.
  3. R/review_weak_matches.R applies rules to the weak DOI matches.
  4. R/prisma_counts_final.R writes the final counts that are shown here.

Our Zotero export holds 12,625 records. After duplicate removal and screening, 11,151 records are included.

PRISMA flow, counted by R/prisma_pipeline.R

3.2.1.1 Duplicates

We removed 1,175 records in four steps. We keep one copy of each work and remove only the extra copies.

  • Same Zotero citekey, exported twice (mostly the same records in documents.bib and reports.bib): 1,100.
  • Same DOI: 7.
  • Same title and year: 53.
  • Same work with a different year or version (preprint and published article, wrong year, garbled author), checked by hand: 15 (data/prisma/duplicates_reviewed.csv).

3.2.1.2 Screening

We removed 257 records marked bin in Zotero, and 42 records by automatic rules (annual reports, syllabi, catalogues, non-scientific sources). Only 89 of the included records were marked read by hand; the rest have not been screened for relevance yet.

3.2.1.3 Crossref check, abstracts and DOIs

We checked every DOI against Crossref (title and year must match). 7,507 of the 11,151 included records are verified. 3,287 have no DOI, so they cannot be checked.

Abstracts: 7,039 of the included records have one (1,994 came from Zotero, 5,045 were added from OpenAlex and Crossref).

# Comprehensive method categories with hierarchical structure
method_categories <- list(

# Enhanced detection function for hierarchical classification
detect_methods_hierarchical <- function(text, categories = method_categories) {
  if(is.na(text) || text == "" || length(text) == 0) return(list())

  text_lower <- tolower(as.character(text))
  detected_methods <- list()

  for(method_name in names(categories)) {
    category_data <- categories[[method_name]]
    all_keywords <- unlist(category_data[c("main_methods", "subcategory_1", "subcategory_2", "subcategory_3")])

    # Create word boundary patterns
    patterns <- paste0("\\b", all_keywords, "\\b")

    # Check for matches
    matches <- str_detect(text_lower, patterns)

    if(any(matches)) {
      matched_keywords <- all_keywords[matches]

      # Classify into subcategories
      main_match <- any(matched_keywords %in% category_data$main_methods)
      sub1_match <- any(matched_keywords %in% category_data$subcategory_1)
      sub2_match <- any(matched_keywords %in% category_data$subcategory_2)
      sub3_match <- any(matched_keywords %in% category_data$subcategory_3)

      detected_methods[[method_name]] <- list(
        main = main_match,
        subcategory_1 = sub1_match,
        subcategory_2 = sub2_match,
        subcategory_3 = sub3_match,
        matched_keywords = matched_keywords,
        description = category_data$description
      )
    }
  }

  return(detected_methods)
}

# Function to get primary method category
get_primary_method <- function(detected_methods_list) {
  if(length(detected_methods_list) == 0) return("No Methods Detected")

  # Prioritize methods with main category matches
  main_matches <- names(detected_methods_list)[sapply(detected_methods_list, function(x) x$main)]

  if(length(main_matches) > 0) {
    return(main_matches[1])  # Return first main match
  } else {
    return(names(detected_methods_list)[1])  # Return first subcategory match
  }
}

5 Data Processing and Analysis

# Load and process bibliographic data
if(exists("bib_data")) {
  # bib_data is built in 03_Data_Import_Pre_Processing.Rmd from the reconciled pipeline (data/prisma/)
  message("Using ", nrow(bib_data), " included records from data/prisma/")

  # Clean and prepare data
  clean_bib_data <- bib_data %>%
    filter(!is.na(TITLE), TITLE != "") %>%
    mutate(
      full_text = paste(
        ifelse(is.na(TITLE), "", TITLE),
        ifelse(is.na(ABSTRACT), "", ABSTRACT),
        ifelse(is.na(KEYWORDS), "", KEYWORDS),
        sep = " "
      ),
      YEAR = as.numeric(YEAR),
      AUTHORS = ifelse(is.na(AUTHOR), "", AUTHOR),
      BIBREF = ifelse(is.na(BIBTEXKEY), paste0("ref_", row_number()), BIBTEXKEY)
    ) %>%
    filter(YEAR >= 1970, YEAR <= 2025) %>%
    filter(!str_detect(tolower(TITLE), "\\b(catalog|syllabus|annual report|bibliography)\\b"))

  message("Processing ", nrow(clean_bib_data), " papers...")

  # Apply hierarchical method detection
  detected_methods_list <- map(clean_bib_data$full_text, detect_methods_hierarchical)

  # Create comprehensive results
  comprehensive_results <- clean_bib_data %>%
    mutate(
      detected_methods = detected_methods_list,
      primary_method = map_chr(detected_methods, get_primary_method),
      has_methods = map_lgl(detected_methods, function(x) length(x) > 0)
    )

  message("Method detection completed: ", sum(comprehensive_results$has_methods), " papers with methods")

} else {
  stop("bib_data not found: 03_Data_Import_Pre_Processing.Rmd must run first")
}

6 Generate CSV Output

# Create the requested CSV with hierarchical method classification
csv_output <- comprehensive_results %>%
  filter(has_methods) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(
    # Get subcategories for primary method
    subcategories = {
      if(primary_method != "No Methods Detected" && primary_method %in% names(detected_methods)) {
        method_data <- detected_methods[[primary_method]]
        subs <- character()

        if(method_data$subcategory_1) {
          sub1_keywords <- intersect(method_data$matched_keywords,
                                   method_categories[[primary_method]]$subcategory_1)
          if(length(sub1_keywords) > 0) subs <- c(subs, sub1_keywords[1])
        }

        if(method_data$subcategory_2) {
          sub2_keywords <- intersect(method_data$matched_keywords,
                                   method_categories[[primary_method]]$subcategory_2)
          if(length(sub2_keywords) > 0) subs <- c(subs, sub2_keywords[1])
        }

        if(method_data$subcategory_3) {
          sub3_keywords <- intersect(method_data$matched_keywords,
                                   method_categories[[primary_method]]$subcategory_3)
          if(length(sub3_keywords) > 0) subs <- c(subs, sub3_keywords[1])
        }

        # Pad with empty strings to ensure 3 subcategories
        list(c(subs, rep("", 3))[1:3])
      } else {
        list(c("", "", ""))
      }
    },

    method_description = {
      if(primary_method != "No Methods Detected" && primary_method %in% names(method_categories)) {
        method_categories[[primary_method]]$description
      } else {
        ""
      }
    }
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(BIBREF, primary_method, subcategories, method_description) %>%
  mutate(
    subcategory_1 = map_chr(subcategories, function(x) x[1]),
    subcategory_2 = map_chr(subcategories, function(x) x[2]),
    subcategory_3 = map_chr(subcategories, function(x) x[3])
  ) %>%
  select(
    bibref = BIBREF,
    main_method_category = primary_method,
    subcategory_1,
    subcategory_2,
    subcategory_3,
    method_description
  )

# Write CSV
write.csv(csv_output, "methods_classification.csv", row.names = FALSE, na = "")

message("Generated methods_classification.csv with ", nrow(csv_output), " classified papers")

7 Sankey Visualizations

# Source the plotting function
source("R/plot_sankey.R")

# Create decade-specific Sankey plots with consistent formatting
create_decade_sankey_consistent <- function(data, target_decade, top_n = 8) {
  decade_data <- data %>%
    mutate(decade = floor(YEAR/10)*10) %>%
    filter(decade == target_decade, has_methods)

  if(nrow(decade_data) == 0) {
    message("No data for decade ", target_decade)
    return(NULL)
  }

  # Count primary methods for this decade
  method_counts <- decade_data %>%
    count(primary_method, sort = TRUE) %>%
    head(top_n)

  total_papers <- nrow(decade_data)

  # Prepare for sankey
  inputs <- c(total_papers, 0)
  losses <- method_counts$n

  # Create consistent labels with fixed text size
  method_labels <- sapply(method_counts$primary_method, function(x) {
    # Intelligent abbreviation for consistency
    if(nchar(x) > 20) {
      words <- str_split(x, "[\\s/]")[[1]]
      if(length(words) > 1) {
        # Take first 3-4 chars of each word
        paste(substr(words[1:min(3, length(words))], 1, 4), collapse = "")
      } else {
        paste0(substr(x, 1, 17), "...")
      }
    } else {
      x
    }
  })

  labels <- c(
    paste0(target_decade, "s\n(n=", format(total_papers, big.mark = ","), ")"),
    "",
    method_labels
  )

  # Set consistent plot parameters
  pdf(paste0("sankey_", target_decade, ".pdf"), width = 10, height = 6)
  par(cex = 0.8, cex.main = 1.0, cex.lab = 0.8, cex.axis = 0.8)

  # Generate the plot with consistent styling
  plot_sankey(inputs, losses, "Papers", labels)

  # Add consistent title
  title(main = paste0("Decision Methods in ", target_decade, "s Literature"),
        cex.main = 1.2, font.main = 2)

  dev.off()

  message("Created Sankey plot for ", target_decade, "s")

  return(list(
    decade = target_decade,
    total_papers = total_papers,
    method_counts = method_counts
  ))
}

# Generate Sankey plots for each decade
decades <- seq(1970, 2020, 10)
sankey_results <- map(decades, ~create_decade_sankey_consistent(comprehensive_results, .x))
names(sankey_results) <- paste0(decades, "s")

# Remove NULL results
sankey_results <- sankey_results[!sapply(sankey_results, is.null)]

# Display decade summaries
decade_summary <- map_dfr(sankey_results, function(x) {
  if(!is.null(x)) {
    data.frame(
      decade = paste0(x$decade, "s"),
      total_papers = x$total_papers,
      top_method = x$method_counts$primary_method[1],
      top_method_count = x$method_counts$n[1]
    )
  }
})

decade_summary %>%
  rename(
    Decade = decade,
    `Total Papers` = total_papers,
    `Top Method` = top_method,
    `Count` = top_method_count
  ) %>%

8 Summary Statistics

# Overall statistics
total_papers <- nrow(comprehensive_results)
papers_with_methods <- sum(comprehensive_results$has_methods)
detection_rate <- round(papers_with_methods / total_papers * 100, 1)

# Method category distribution
method_distribution <- comprehensive_results %>%
  filter(has_methods) %>%
  count(primary_method, sort = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    percentage = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 1)
  )

cat("## Analysis Summary\n\n")

cat("- **Papers with Methods:** ", format(papers_with_methods, big.mark = ","),
    " (", detection_rate, "%)\n")

cat("- **Method Categories:** ", length(method_categories), "\n")
